title: Separating Attack Behavior from Testbed Artifacts in the UNSW-NB15 Intrusion Detection Dataset
thesis: UNSW-NB15 attacks have a measurable traffic fingerprint (small, short flows with family-specific byte sizes), but its host and hourly patterns are lab artifacts; telling them apart requires first integrating the four headerless files and repairing the 13 label spellings.
significance: Anyone training intrusion detectors on this benchmark must use repaired labels and exclude host and time features, or the model learns the testbed instead of the attacks.

2,540,047.means: network flows in the four raw parts together

13.means: distinct raw spellings of the attack-category label

49.means: rows in the dataset's feature-definition file (one per column)

4.means: source hosts that sent any attack flow

3,977.means: citations of the UNSW-NB15 source paper (OpenAlex, checked 2026-10-07)

2023.means: year of Zoghi & Serpen's analysis as cited in the locked sentence (journal version; arXiv preprint 2021)

312.means: port values in the raw parts that are not decimal numbers (hexadecimal or '-')

2.6.means: speed-up of the database path over reading the raw parts for the H2 query (15.0 s vs 5.8 s, one recorded run)

4.1.means: DataFrame memory ratio, raw parts vs database join (1,980 MB vs 483 MB)

0.991.means: area under the ROC curve of the rule 'flow comes from an attacking host' (H6)

0.865.means: area under the ROC curve of source bytes alone (H6)

background.text: Intrusion detection is widely evaluated on UNSW-NB15, a benchmark built in a University of New South Wales lab (its source paper has 3,977 citations); prior analysis found class imbalance and overlap (Zoghi & Serpen, 2023), but inconsistent labels and testbed patterns that can be seen as attack behavior require attention.
background.intent: Intrusion detection is evaluated on UNSW-NB15 (3,977 citations); prior work found imbalance and overlap; two shortcomings need attention: inconsistent labels and testbed patterns seen as attack behavior. Word order changed by the instructor (2026-10-07) so the purpose comes before the dataset name.

prior.intent: Zoghi & Serpen found class imbalance and class overlap in UNSW-NB15.

G1.intent: Problem 1: the raw files cannot be read or counted correctly as delivered.

G2.intent: Problem 2: lab patterns can pass for attack behavior.

problem.text: Its 2,540,047 flows are in four headerless files, with 13 label spellings for 9 families. We constructed a third-normal-form SQLite database from its 49-row definition file, decoding ports and repairing labels.
problem.intent: Four headerless files, 13 spellings for 9 families; a third-normal-form database built from the definition file, ports decoded, labels repaired.

solution.intent: Schema from the 49-row definition file; ports decoded; labels repaired.

why.text: Compared with the raw files, the database contains 9 attack families instead of 13 groups (Fuzzers split 19,195 + 5,051), identifies 312 non-decimal ports, and computes family medians 2.6x faster with 4.1x less memory.
why.intent: Against the raw files the database counts 9 families not 13 groups, catches 312 bad ports, and is 2.2x faster with 4.1x less memory.

question.intent: Do attack flows differ from normal ones, and which patterns are behavior vs lab artifacts?

extract.intent: SQL joins load eight typed columns into pandas; effect size decides because all p-values are tiny.

test_why.intent: All five tests reach p < 0.001, so effect size decides.

alternative.intent: Raw labels give 13 groups instead of 9 families.

form.intent: Log-scale boxplots of source bytes by family.

finding.text: Attack flows are clearly smaller and shorter than normal ones, families vary strongly in byte size, and service is moderately related to attacks.
finding.intent: Secondary results in words: H1 large (rank-biserial r 0.73 bytes, 0.55 duration), H2 strong (epsilon-squared 0.76), H3 moderate (Cramer's V 0.30).

G1.intent: The database fixes the raw-file problems, measured against the raw files.
G1.baseline: the four raw CSV parts read as delivered
G1.measure: attack groups counted (13 vs 9), non-decimal ports caught (312), query time (15.0 s vs 5.8 s, one recorded run), DataFrame memory (1,980 MB vs 483 MB)

G2.text: However, linking each flow to its source host, we found all attacks are from 4 of 43 hosts; a rule that flags those hosts' flows, a shortcut any trained detector can learn, achieves an area under the ROC curve of 0.991, above source bytes at 0.865, and hourly attack shares (0% to 28.8%) likely follow the testbed schedule.
G2.intent: Host concentration and the hourly pattern come from the testbed, not behavior.
G2.baseline: a behavior feature (source bytes) used alone
G2.measure: area under the ROC curve of one-feature rules: host 0.991 vs source bytes 0.865; hourly attack share 0% to 28.8%

value.intent: Separating behavior from lab artifacts tells model builders which features to drop.

conclusion.text: Byte and duration profiles represent attack behavior; host and time features may cause detectors to learn testbed artifacts.
conclusion.intent: Byte and duration profiles are behavior; host and time features risk teaching the lab.

future.text: Next, scikit-learn and TensorFlow classifiers without those features will be evaluated per family on F1 and area under the curve.
future.intent: Next: classifiers without host and time features, scored per family by F1 and area under the curve.
